claim: The mammalian imprinted Dlk1-Dio3 locus produces multiple long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) from the maternally inherited allele, including Meg3 (i.e., Gtl2) in the mammalian genome.
source: The mammalian imprinted Dlk1-Dio3 locus produces multiple long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) from the maternally inherited allele, including Meg3 (i.e., Gtl2) in the mammalian genome.
evidence: This is a well-established fact about the Dlk1-Dio3 locus structure and is supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: lncRNAs expressed from the Dlk1-Dio3 locus are predominantly and gradually enriched in rostral motor neurons (MNs).
source: we uncovered that lncRNAs expressed from the Dlk1-Dio3 locus are predominantly and gradually enriched in rostral motor neurons (MNs).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data, in situ hybridization, and qPCR experiments shown in the manuscript.

claim: Meg3 and other Dlk1-Dio3 locus-derived lncRNAs facilitate Ezh2/Jarid2 interactions.
source: Mechanistically, Meg3 and other Dlk1-Dio3 locus-derived lncRNAs facilitate Ezh2/Jarid2 interactions.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments and RNA immunoprecipitation assays shown in Figure 3.

claim: Loss of Dlk1-Dio3 locus-derived lncRNAs compromises the H3K27me3 landscape.
source: Loss of these lncRNAs compromises the H3K27me3 landscape, leading to aberrant expression of progenitor and caudal Hox genes in postmitotic MNs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-seq data comparing control and Meg3 KD or IG-DMRmatΔ ESC-MNs shown in Figure 4.

claim: Loss of Dlk1-Dio3 locus-derived lncRNAs leads to aberrant expression of progenitor genes in postmitotic MNs.
source: Loss of these lncRNAs compromises the H3K27me3 landscape, leading to aberrant expression of progenitor and caudal Hox genes in postmitotic MNs.
evidence: This is supported by microarray data, qPCR, and immunostaining showing upregulation of Pax6 and Irx3 in Meg3 KD and IG-DMRmatΔ MNs.

claim: Loss of Dlk1-Dio3 locus-derived lncRNAs leads to aberrant expression of caudal Hox genes in postmitotic MNs.
source: Loss of these lncRNAs compromises the H3K27me3 landscape, leading to aberrant expression of progenitor and caudal Hox genes in postmitotic MNs.
evidence: This is supported by microarray data, qPCR, and immunostaining showing upregulation of Hox8-13 genes in Meg3 KD and IG-DMRmatΔ MNs.

claim: lncRNAs in the Dlk1-Dio3 locus play a critical role in maintaining postmitotic MN cell fate by repressing progenitor genes.
source: Our data thus illustrate that these lncRNAs in the Dlk1-Dio3 locus, particularly Meg3, play a critical role in maintaining postmitotic MN cell fate by repressing progenitor genes and they shape MN subtype identity by regulating Hox genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that loss of these lncRNAs leads to ectopic expression of progenitor genes in postmitotic MNs.

claim: lncRNAs in the Dlk1-Dio3 locus shape MN subtype identity by regulating Hox genes.
source: Our data thus illustrate that these lncRNAs in the Dlk1-Dio3 locus, particularly Meg3, play a critical role in maintaining postmitotic MN cell fate by repressing progenitor genes and they shape MN subtype identity by regulating Hox genes.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that loss of these lncRNAs leads to dysregulation of Hox gene expression and altered motor pool identity.

claim: Non-coding RNAs account for at least 50~80% of mammalian transcriptomes.
source: However, given the prevalence of high-throughput sequencing analyses of mammalian genomes, it is now appreciated that non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) account for at least 50~80% of transcriptomes (Pauli et al., 2011; Rinn and Chang, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Approximately 20% of lncRNAs are associated with polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2).
source: Approximately 20% of lncRNAs are associated with polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2) (Zhao et al., 2010; Khalil et al., 2009), which is comprised of many subunits and functions to deposit histone H3K27 trimethylation (H3K27me3) and to suppress gene expression (Di Croce and Helin, 2013; Margueron and Reinberg, 2011; Simon and Kingston, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: PRC2 is comprised of many subunits and functions to deposit histone H3K27 trimethylation (H3K27me3) and to suppress gene expression.
source: Approximately 20% of lncRNAs are associated with polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2) (Zhao et al., 2010; Khalil et al., 2009), which is comprised of many subunits and functions to deposit histone H3K27 trimethylation (H3K27me3) and to suppress gene expression (Di Croce and Helin, 2013; Margueron and Reinberg, 2011; Simon and Kingston, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PRC2 function supported by citations.

claim: Segmental identity of MNs is defined by the mutually exclusive expression of Hox6, Hox9 and Hox10.
source: For example, segmental identity of MNs is defined by the mutually exclusive expression of Hox6, Hox9 and Hox10 (Dasen et al., 2003; Lacombe et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on motor neuron development.

claim: Within the brachial Hox6on segment, MNs are further grouped into axial muscle projecting MNs (Lhx3on, MMC) and forelimb-innervating MNs (Foxp1on, LMC).
source: For instance, within the brachial Hox6on segment, MNs are further grouped into axial muscle projecting MNs (Lhx3on, MMC) and forelimb-innervating MNs (Foxp1on, LMC).
evidence: This is established knowledge about motor neuron columnar organization.

claim: Hox5 and Hox8 expression in the Foxp1on LMC controls the rostral and caudal motor pool identity.
source: Finally, another set of mutually exclusive Hox proteins, such as Hox5 and Hox8 expression in the Foxp1on LMC, further controls the rostral and caudal motor pool identity, which directs motor pools to either innervate proximal or distal muscles in the forelimb (Catela et al., 2016; Dasen et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies on motor pool specification.

claim: Depletion of the polycomb repressive complex 1 (PRC1) component Bmi1 at brachial level causes ectopic expression of Hoxc9 and subjects LMC neurons to a thoracic preganglionic column (PGC) fate.
source: Depletion of the polycomb repressive complex 1 (PRC1) component Bmi1 at brachial level causes ectopic expression of Hoxc9 and subjects LMC neurons to a thoracic preganglionic column (PGC) fate.
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study that is being cited to provide context.

claim: Elevation of Bmi1 represses Hoxc9 at thoracic level and subjects PGC neurons to an LMC fate.
source: Conversely, elevation of Bmi1 represses Hoxc9 at thoracic level and subjects PGC neurons to an LMC fate (Golden and Dasen, 2012).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study that is being cited to provide context.

claim: RA activates retinoic acid receptors (RARs) and binds to the Hox1~5 chromatin domains, which is followed by synchronous domain-wide removal of H3K27me3 to acquire cervical spinal identity.
source: More specifically, RA activates retinoic acid receptors (RARs) and binds to the Hox1~5 chromatin domains, which is followed by synchronous domain-wide removal of H3K27me3 to acquire cervical spinal identity.
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study that is being cited to provide context.

claim: A gradient of Wnt and FGF signals induces expression of the Cdx2 transcription factor that binds and clears H3K27me3 from the Hox1~Hox9 chromatin domains, thereby establishing brachial or thoracic segmental identity.
source: At the tailbud, a gradient of Wnt and FGF signals induces expression of the Cdx2 transcription factor that binds and clears H3K27me3 from the Hox1~Hox9 chromatin domains, thereby establishing brachial or thoracic segmental identity (Mazzoni et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study that is being cited to provide context.

claim: The Dlk1-Dio3 locus contains three protein-coding genes (Dlk1, Rtl1, and Dio3) from the paternally inherited allele.
source: The Dlk1-Dio3 locus contains three protein-coding genes (Dlk1, Rtl1, and Dio3) from the paternally inherited allele, and multiple lncRNAs and small ncRNAs are derived from the maternally inherited allele, including Meg3, Rian (containing 22 box C/D snoRNAs), as well as the largest miRNA mega-cluster in mammals (anti-Rtl1, which contains the miR-127/miR-136 cluster of 7 miRNAs, and Mirg that within the miR-379/miR-410 cluster).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Dlk1-Dio3 locus structure.

claim: Multiple lncRNAs and small ncRNAs are derived from the maternally inherited allele of the Dlk1-Dio3 locus, including Meg3, Rian (containing 22 box C/D snoRNAs), as well as the largest miRNA mega-cluster in mammals.
source: The Dlk1-Dio3 locus contains three protein-coding genes (Dlk1, Rtl1, and Dio3) from the paternally inherited allele, and multiple lncRNAs and small ncRNAs are derived from the maternally inherited allele, including Meg3, Rian (containing 22 box C/D snoRNAs), as well as the largest miRNA mega-cluster in mammals (anti-Rtl1, which contains the miR-127/miR-136 cluster of 7 miRNAs, and Mirg that within the miR-379/miR-410 cluster).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Dlk1-Dio3 locus structure.

claim: All of the ncRNAs in the Dlk1-Dio3 locus are regulated by a common cis-element and epigenetic control, resulting in a presumable large polycistronic transcription unit.
source: Interestingly, all of the ncRNAs are regulated by a common cis-element and epigenetic control, resulting in a presumable large polycistronic transcription unit (Das et al., 2015; Lin et al., 2003; Seitz et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The Dlk1-Dio3 locus is well known to play crucial roles in stem cells.
source: Although the Dlk1-Dio3 locus is well known to play crucial roles in stem cells (Lin et al., 2007; Lin et al., 2003; Qian et al., 2016), we unexpectedly found that expressions of Meg3 and other lncRNAs from the Dlk1-Dio3 locus are also all enriched in postmitotic MNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Expressions of Meg3 and other lncRNAs from the Dlk1-Dio3 locus are all enriched in postmitotic MNs.
source: Although the Dlk1-Dio3 locus is well known to play crucial roles in stem cells (Lin et al., 2007; Lin et al., 2003; Qian et al., 2016), we unexpectedly found that expressions of Meg3 and other lncRNAs from the Dlk1-Dio3 locus are also all enriched in postmitotic MNs.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study supported by RNA-seq, qPCR, and in situ hybridization data.

claim: An ESC line harbouring the MN transgenic reporter Hb9::GFP was harnessed into MNs.
source: Firstly, an ESC line harbouring the MN transgenic reporter Hb9::GFP was harnessed into MNs (Wichterle et al., 2002), and we then sequentially collected RA-induced nascent neural epithelia (Hoxa1on, NE at day 2), MN progenitors (Olig2on, pMN at day 4), and postmitotic MNs (Hb9::GFPon, postmitotic MNs at day 7) by fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: RA-induced nascent neural epithelia (Hoxa1on, NE at day 2), MN progenitors (Olig2on, pMN at day 4), and postmitotic MNs (Hb9::GFPon, postmitotic MNs at day 7) were sequentially collected by fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS).
source: Firstly, an ESC line harbouring the MN transgenic reporter Hb9::GFP was harnessed into MNs (Wichterle et al., 2002), and we then sequentially collected RA-induced nascent neural epithelia (Hoxa1on, NE at day 2), MN progenitors (Olig2on, pMN at day 4), and postmitotic MNs (Hb9::GFPon, postmitotic MNs at day 7) by fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Strand-specific RNA-seq was performed across libraries preserving non-polyadenylated transcripts while removing ribosomal RNAs.
source: Next, we performed strand-specific RNA-seq across libraries preserving non-polyadenylated transcripts while removing ribosomal RNAs, since many lncRNAs are non-polyadenylated (Yin et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2012), and carried out de novo transcriptome assembly (Qian et al., 2016) to discover novel lncRNAs that might be specifically enriched during MN development (detailed in the Materials and methods and summarized in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Many lncRNAs are non-polyadenylated.
source: Next, we performed strand-specific RNA-seq across libraries preserving non-polyadenylated transcripts while removing ribosomal RNAs, since many lncRNAs are non-polyadenylated (Yin et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2012), and carried out de novo transcriptome assembly (Qian et al., 2016) to discover novel lncRNAs that might be specifically enriched during MN development (detailed in the Materials and methods and summarized in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Several known markers for each cell type during MN differentiation were accurately recovered, corroborating the high quality and specificity of the RNA-seq data.
source: Several known markers for each cell type during MN differentiation were accurately recovered, corroborating the high quality and specificity of our RNA-seq data (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the heatmap in Figure 1B showing expression of known transcription factors.

claim: The RNA-seq approach yielded 10,177 lncRNAs, 752 of which (7.39%) were previously unidentified from the Ensemble mm10 database.
source: Our approach yielded 10,177 lncRNAs, 752 of which (7.39%) were previously unidentified from the Ensemble mm10 database.
evidence: This is a direct result from the RNA-seq analysis performed in the study.

claim: 4295 (77.78%) of the identified lncRNAs overlapped with recently reported spinal MN-related lncRNAs discovered by poly A+-enriched RNA-seq approaches.
source: We also found that 4295 (77.78%) of our identified lncRNAs overlapped with recently reported spinal MN-related lncRNAs, which were discovered by poly A+-enriched RNA-seq approaches (Amin et al., 2015; Narendra et al., 2015) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a comparison of the current study's results with previously published data.

claim: 70 stage-signature lncRNAs during the ESC~MNs differentiation process were uncovered.
source: Based on stage-specific scores (see Materials and methods), 70 stage-signature lncRNAs during the ESC~MNs differentiation process were uncovered (ESC, NE, pMN, MN, and IN in Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a result from the RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Compared to protein-coding genes, both annotated lncRNAs and novel lncRNAs had higher cell-type specificity.
source: Compared to protein-coding genes, both annotated lncRNAs and novel lncRNAs (newly identified in our de novo transcriptome assembly) had higher cell-type specificity (Figure 1D, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, p=1.41 × 10−9 and p=3.53 × 10−7, respectively; see Materials and methods), implying that lncRNAs might play specific roles in each cell type during ESC~MN differentiation.
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: lncRNAs might play specific roles in each cell type during ESC~MN differentiation.
source: Compared to protein-coding genes, both annotated lncRNAs and novel lncRNAs (newly identified in our de novo transcriptome assembly) had higher cell-type specificity (Figure 1D, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, p=1.41 × 10−9 and p=3.53 × 10−7, respectively; see Materials and methods), implying that lncRNAs might play specific roles in each cell type during ESC~MN differentiation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that lncRNAs have higher cell-type specificity.

claim: 117 lncRNA candidates were identified as being postmitotic MN-enriched.
source: We identified 117 lncRNA candidates from our analysis as being postmitotic MN-enriched.
evidence: This is a result from the RNA-seq analysis comparing different cell types.

claim: The lncRNAs Meg3, Rian, and Mirg, which are transcribed from the imprinted Dlk1-Dio3 locus on mouse chromosome 12qF, all manifested strong enrichment in postmitotic MNs.
source: Interestingly, the lncRNAs Meg3, Rian, and Mirg, which are transcribed from the imprinted Dlk1-Dio3 locus on mouse chromosome 12qF, all manifested strong enrichment in postmitotic MNs (simplified schematic locus depicted in Figure 2C, detailed locus information in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2A and 2B, as well as qPCR validation.

claim: The lncRNAs from the Dlk1-Dio3 locus are conserved amongst placental mammals.
source: Since these lncRNAs are conserved amongst placental mammals (Ogata and Kagami, 2016), we chose to characterize their functions in greater detail.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: An MN-specific active chromatin region with enhancer/promoter characteristics and direct MN-specific transcription factor binding was uncovered within the Meg3-Rian-Mirg locus.
source: Within this locus, we uncovered an MN-specific active chromatin region that possesses enhancer/promoter characteristics with direct MN-specific transcription factor binding (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on analysis of published ChIP-seq and ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Overexpression of MN-TFs in a maternally-inherited intergenic differentially methylated region deletion (IG-DMRmatΔ) ESC line can robustly induce Meg3 expression.
source: Furthermore, overexpression of MN-TFs in a maternally-inherited intergenic differentially methylated region deletion (IG-DMRmatΔ) ESC line, which leads to simultaneous silencing of all maternally-expressed lncRNAs in the Meg3-Rian-Mirg locus but leaves the MN-TF binding site intact (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) (Lin et al., 2007; Lin et al., 2003), can robustly induce Meg3 expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: MN-TFs bind and directly activate Meg3 during ESC~MN differentiation.
source: Therefore, we suggest that MN-TFs bind and directly activate Meg3 during ESC~MN differentiation.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP-seq data and the overexpression experiments.

claim: Meg3 expression is enriched in the mantle zone of the developing spinal cord during development and is gradually enriched in postmitotic MNs (Isl1/2on cells) after E12.5.
source: We found that Meg3 expression: (1) is enriched in the mantle zone of the developing spinal cord during development and is gradually enriched in postmitotic MNs (Isl1/2on cells) after E12.5; (2) has no preference for columnar MN subtypes, as revealed by Foxp1 (LMC-MNs) and Lhx3 (MMC-MNs) immunostaining; and (3) exhibits rostral high (brachial and thoracic) and caudal low (lumbar) asymmetry after E12.5 (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization and immunostaining data shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: Meg3 has no preference for columnar MN subtypes.
source: We found that Meg3 expression: (1) is enriched in the mantle zone of the developing spinal cord during development and is gradually enriched in postmitotic MNs (Isl1/2on cells) after E12.5; (2) has no preference for columnar MN subtypes, as revealed by Foxp1 (LMC-MNs) and Lhx3 (MMC-MNs) immunostaining; and (3) exhibits rostral high (brachial and thoracic) and caudal low (lumbar) asymmetry after E12.5 (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization and immunostaining data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Meg3 exhibits rostral high (brachial and thoracic) and caudal low (lumbar) asymmetry after E12.5.
source: We found that Meg3 expression: (1) is enriched in the mantle zone of the developing spinal cord during development and is gradually enriched in postmitotic MNs (Isl1/2on cells) after E12.5; (2) has no preference for columnar MN subtypes, as revealed by Foxp1 (LMC-MNs) and Lhx3 (MMC-MNs) immunostaining; and (3) exhibits rostral high (brachial and thoracic) and caudal low (lumbar) asymmetry after E12.5 (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: RA treatment results in novel binding of RAR directly to the Meg3 promoter, as well as subsequent recruitment of the basal transcription complex (Pol2-S5P).
source: Interestingly, we found that RA treatment results in novel binding of RAR directly to the Meg3 promoter, as well as subsequent recruitment of the basal transcription complex (Pol2-S5P in Figure 2H).
evidence: This is based on analysis of published ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2G and H.

claim: Meg3 is induced after the addition of RA in IG-DMRmatΔ ESCs after 8 hr.
source: Moreover, we observed that Meg3 is induced after the addition of RA in IG-DMRmatΔ ESCs after 8 hr (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), indicating that RA/RAR activation triggers the strong Meg3 expression in rostral brachial MNs.
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: RA/RAR activation triggers the strong Meg3 expression in rostral brachial MNs.
source: Moreover, we observed that Meg3 is induced after the addition of RA in IG-DMRmatΔ ESCs after 8 hr (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), indicating that RA/RAR activation triggers the strong Meg3 expression in rostral brachial MNs.
evidence: This is inferred from the RA induction experiment and the rostral enrichment of Meg3.

claim: Meg3 exhibits a speckled pattern of expression enriched in the nucleus.
source: We observed a speckled pattern of Meg3 expression enriched in the nucleus, suggesting it has a potential function in gene regulation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is based on single molecule RNA FISH data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Meg3 is not only enriched in the nucleus, but is also chromatin-associated.
source: Furthermore, qPCR of subcellular-fractionated RNAs from ESC~MNs validated that Meg3 is not only enriched in the nucleus, but that it is also chromatin-associated (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E; Gapdh as cytoplasmic marker, Rnu1 (U1 snRNA) as nuclear marker, and Kcnq1ot1 as a chromatin-associated RNA control).
evidence: This is based on subcellular fractionation and qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: lncRNAs in the Dlk1-Dio3 locus are postmitotic MN-enriched, and they are directly activated by MN-TFs and RA/RAR.
source: Together, these findings suggest that lncRNAs in the Dlk1-Dio3 locus are postmitotic MN-enriched, and that they are directly activated by MN-TFs and RA/RAR.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the experiments described in the Results section.

claim: Meg3 is highly enriched in MN nuclei and is chromatin-associated, indicating a potential function in chromatin regulation.
source: At a cellular level, Meg3 is highly enriched in MN nuclei and is chromatin-associated, indicating a potential function in chromatin regulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the subcellular localization data.

claim: Interactions between Jarid2 and ncRNAs regulate PRC2 recruitment to chromatin, including lncRNAs in the Dlk1-Dio3 locus of ESCs.
source: While several previous reports have revealed that interactions between Jarid2 and ncRNAs regulate PRC2 recruitment to chromatin, including lncRNAs in the Dlk1-Dio3 locus of ESCs (da Rocha et al., 2014; Kaneko et al., 2014a; Kaneko et al., 2014b), the roles of PRC2/Jarid2 in postmitotic cells are less clear.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Expression of Jarid2 was reactivated in postmitotic MNs.
source: Surprisingly, we found that expression of Jarid2 was reactivated in postmitotic MNs, pointing to a possible specific regulation in this cell type (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A upper panel) (Takeuchi et al., 1995).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Meg3 and Rian manifested much more abundant expressions in the postmitotic MNs compared to several known lncRNAs that interact with PRC2 complex.
source: Moreover, compared to several known lncRNAs that interact with PRC2 complex, Meg3 and Rian manifested much more abundant expressions in the postmitotic MNs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A lower panel).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Immunoprecipitation (IP) of endogenous PRC2 complex components (i.e., Ezh2 and Suz12), as well as the PRC2 cofactor Jarid2, from ESC~MNs specifically retrieves Meg3, Rian and Mirg RNA.
source: To test this hypothesis, we first demonstrated that immunoprecipitation (IP) of endogenous PRC2 complex components (i.e., Ezh2 and Suz12), as well as the PRC2 cofactor Jarid2, from ESC~MNs specifically retrieves Meg3, Rian and Mirg RNA, whereas the nuclear ncRNA Rnu1 and the lncRNA Malat1 were not captured by Ezh2, Jarid2, or Suz12 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on RNA immunoprecipitation (RIP) data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The nuclear ncRNA Rnu1 and the lncRNA Malat1 were not captured by Ezh2, Jarid2, or Suz12.
source: To test this hypothesis, we first demonstrated that immunoprecipitation (IP) of endogenous PRC2 complex components (i.e., Ezh2 and Suz12), as well as the PRC2 cofactor Jarid2, from ESC~MNs specifically retrieves Meg3, Rian and Mirg RNA, whereas the nuclear ncRNA Rnu1 and the lncRNA Malat1 were not captured by Ezh2, Jarid2, or Suz12 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on RNA immunoprecipitation (RIP) data shown in Figure 3A, serving as negative controls.

claim: Two isoforms, Meg3v1 and Meg3v5, are predominantly expressed in Hb9::GFPon MNs.
source: Several Meg3 isoforms have previously been documented, so we scrutinized across the entire Meg3 locus (~31 kb) and found that two isoforms, Meg3v1 and Meg3v5 (Ensemble mm10 database), are predominantly expressed in Hb9::GFPon MNs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Meg3v1 and Meg3v5 isoforms account for more than 99% of Meg3 transcripts during ESC~MN differentiation.
source: Moreover, Meg3v1 and Meg3v5 isoforms account for more than 99% of Meg3 transcripts than other isoforms during ESC~MN differentiation. (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D) (Kaneko et al., 2014b; Zhou et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Meg3v1 and Meg3v5 have mutually exclusive exon sequences.
source: Interestingly, Meg3v1 and Meg3v5 have mutually exclusive exon sequences (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), raising the possibility that the two isoforms might exert different functions.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the Meg3 locus structure shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Both purified biotinylated Meg3v1 and Meg3v5 RNA retrieved Ezh2 from cell nuclear extracts of ESC~MNs.
source: However, both purified biotinylated Meg3v1 and Meg3v5 RNA retrieved Ezh2 from cell nuclear extracts of ESC~MNs (Figure 3B; GFP RNA was used as a negative control).
evidence: This is based on RNA pull-down assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Meg3 isoforms directly interact with PRC2/Jarid2 complexes and might facilitate association of the PRC2 complex with Jarid2.
source: These results suggest that these Meg3 isoforms directly interact with PRC2/Jarid2 complexes and might facilitate association of the PRC2 complex with Jarid2.
evidence: This is inferred from the RIP and RNA pull-down data.

claim: Meg3 knockdown (KD) did not affect the protein abundance of Ezh2/Jarid2.
source: We first verified that Meg3 knockdown (KD) did not affect the protein abundance of Ezh2/Jarid2, but we did observe that it undermined the interaction between Ezh2 and Jarid2, suggesting that Meg3 facilitates this interaction (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is based on Western blot data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Meg3 knockdown undermined the interaction between Ezh2 and Jarid2.
source: We first verified that Meg3 knockdown (KD) did not affect the protein abundance of Ezh2/Jarid2, but we did observe that it undermined the interaction between Ezh2 and Jarid2, suggesting that Meg3 facilitates this interaction (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is based on co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Meg3 facilitates the interaction between Ezh2 and Jarid2.
source: We first verified that Meg3 knockdown (KD) did not affect the protein abundance of Ezh2/Jarid2, but we did observe that it undermined the interaction between Ezh2 and Jarid2, suggesting that Meg3 facilitates this interaction (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Meg3 KD reduces Ezh2-Jarid2 interaction.

claim: Upon doxycycline induction, both Meg3 isoforms were induced ~20–50 fold, yet the abundance of Ezh2/Jarid2 remained unaffected.
source: Upon doxycycline induction, both Meg3 isoforms were induced ~20–50 fold, yet the abundance of Ezh2/Jarid2 remained unaffected (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is based on qPCR and Western blot data from the inducible Meg3 ESC lines shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: Meg3v5 overexpression in ESC~MNs significantly increased the binding of Ezh2 and Jarid2.
source: Meg3v5 overexpression in ESC~MNs significantly increased the binding of Ezh2 and Jarid2, whereas Meg3v1 overexpression Figure 3E; Figure 3F had a minimal effect (Figure 3G), indicating that Meg3v5 is a strong facilitator of the binding of the PRC2 complex and Jarid2.
evidence: This is based on co-immunoprecipitation data from the inducible Meg3 ESC lines shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Meg3v1 overexpression had a minimal effect on the binding of Ezh2 and Jarid2.
source: Meg3v5 overexpression in ESC~MNs significantly increased the binding of Ezh2 and Jarid2, whereas Meg3v1 overexpression Figure 3E; Figure 3F had a minimal effect (Figure 3G), indicating that Meg3v5 is a strong facilitator of the binding of the PRC2 complex and Jarid2.
evidence: This is based on co-immunoprecipitation data from the inducible Meg3 ESC lines shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Meg3v5 is a strong facilitator of the binding of the PRC2 complex and Jarid2.
source: Meg3v5 overexpression in ESC~MNs significantly increased the binding of Ezh2 and Jarid2, whereas Meg3v1 overexpression Figure 3E; Figure 3F had a minimal effect (Figure 3G), indicating that Meg3v5 is a strong facilitator of the binding of the PRC2 complex and Jarid2.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of Meg3v1 and Meg3v5 overexpression on Ezh2-Jarid2 interaction.

claim: Two retrovirus-based short hairpin RNAs (shRNAs) targeting Meg3 reduced the expression of Meg3 by an average of ~90% compared to endogenous levels in ESC~MNs.
source: To overcome the complication of concomitant up-regulation of paternal coding genes in IG-DMRmatΔ ESCs (Lin et al., 2007; Lin et al., 2003), we further established two retrovirus-based short hairpin RNAs (shRNAs) targeting Meg3 and used a knockdown approach to prevent impairment of DMR sites. Both shRNAs reduced the expression of Meg3 by an average of ~90% compared to endogenous levels in ESC~MNs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The expressions of two other lncRNAs, Rian and Mirg, from the maternal allele of the Dlk1-Dio3 imprinted locus were all significantly down-regulated in Meg3 KD MNs.
source: Verification by qPCR indicated that the expressions of two other lncRNAs, Rian and Mirg, from the maternal allele of the Dlk1-Dio3 imprinted locus were all significantly down-regulated in Meg3 KD MNs, whereas paternal genes were unaffected (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Paternal genes were unaffected in Meg3 KD MNs.
source: Verification by qPCR indicated that the expressions of two other lncRNAs, Rian and Mirg, from the maternal allele of the Dlk1-Dio3 imprinted locus were all significantly down-regulated in Meg3 KD MNs, whereas paternal genes were unaffected (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Meg3-Rian-Mirg probably represents a single continuous transcriptional unit.
source: This finding is consistent with a previous report indicating that Meg3-Rian-Mirg probably represents a single continuous transcriptional unit (Das et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study and is consistent with the observation that Meg3 KD affects Rian and Mirg expression.

claim: A trend of global down-regulation of H3K27me3 was observed in both independent experiments of Meg3 KD MNs.
source: We then performed H3K27me3 ChIP-seq of control and Meg3 KD MNs. We observed a trend of global down-regulation of H3K27me3 in both independent experiments of Meg3 KD MNs, most likely a reflection of compromised Ezh2/Jarid2 interaction (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 585 genes in MNs displayed down-regulation of the H3K27me3 epigenetic landscape and concomitant up-regulation of gene expression upon loss of the Meg3 lncRNAs.
source: This approach revealed 585 genes in MNs that displayed down-regulation of the H3K27me3 epigenetic landscape and concomitant up-regulation of gene expression upon loss of the Meg3 lncRNAs (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on integrated analysis of ChIP-seq and microarray data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Gene ontology (GO) analysis of the 585 genes revealed significant enrichment for RC patterning and progenitor genes, and strikingly so for homeodomain Hox genes.
source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis of these genes revealed significant enrichment for RC patterning and progenitor genes, and strikingly so for homeodomain Hox genes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D; false discovery rate (FDR) q-value ≤0.05).
evidence: This is based on GO analysis of the dysregulated genes shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: MN progenitor (Pax6 and Irx3) and majority of caudal Hox genes (Hox8~13) were up-regulated with a concomitant down-regulation of the H3K27me3 epigenetic landscape.
source: Subsequently, we observed that MN progenitor (Pax6 and Irx3) and majority of caudal Hox genes (Hox8~13) were up-regulated with a concomitant down-regulation of the H3K27me3 epigenetic landscape (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is based on integrated analysis of ChIP-seq and microarray data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: All Meg3 KD ESC~MNs exhibited imbalanced expression of 3' and 5' Hox genes across entire Hox clusters.
source: We corroborated this finding by generating a third Meg3 KD ESC line (I6) and confirming that all Meg3 KD ESC~MNs exhibited imbalanced expression of 3' and 5' Hox genes across entire Hox clusters (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is based on qPCR data from three independent Meg3 KD lines shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: For both Meg3 KD and IG-DMRmatΔ ESC~MNs, dysregulation of progenitor and caudal Hox gene expression is apparent, likely due to loss of the robustness of the epigenetic landscape of postmitotic MNs.
source: Thus, for both Meg3 KD and IG-DMRmatΔ ESC~MNs, dysregulation of progenitor and caudal Hox gene expression is apparent, likely due to loss of the robustness of the epigenetic landscape of postmitotic MNs.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the ChIP-seq and gene expression data.

claim: The epigenetic landscapes of H3K27me3 in the progenitor and caudal Hox genes are concordant with Ezh2 enrichment.
source: Consistent with our prediction, we verified that (1) the epigenetic landscapes of H3K27me3 in the progenitor and caudal Hox genes uncovered here are concordant with Ezh2 enrichment revealed by a previous study that used the same ESC~MN differentiation approach to generate cervical Hoxa5on MNs (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B) (Narendra et al., 2015); (2) Upon Meg3 KD, the bindings of Ezh2/Jaird2 to progenitor (i.e., Pax6 and Irx3) and caudal Hox (i.e., Hoxc8) genes were concomitantly reduced (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: This is based on comparison with published ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: Upon Meg3 KD, the bindings of Ezh2/Jarid2 to progenitor (i.e., Pax6 and Irx3) and caudal Hox (i.e., Hoxc8) genes were concomitantly reduced.
source: Consistent with our prediction, we verified that (1) the epigenetic landscapes of H3K27me3 in the progenitor and caudal Hox genes uncovered here are concordant with Ezh2 enrichment revealed by a previous study that used the same ESC~MN differentiation approach to generate cervical Hoxa5on MNs (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B) (Narendra et al., 2015); (2) Upon Meg3 KD, the bindings of Ezh2/Jaird2 to progenitor (i.e., Pax6 and Irx3) and caudal Hox (i.e., Hoxc8) genes were concomitantly reduced (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: This is based on ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C–E.

claim: Meg3 bridges the PRC2/Jarid2 complex to perpetuate the rostral MN cell fate by silencing epigenetic state of MN progenitor and caudal Hox genes.
source: Taken all together, these results suggest that Meg3 bridges the PRC2/Jarid2 complex to perpetuate the rostral MN cell fate by silencing epigenetic state of MN progenitor and caudal Hox genes.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on all the ChIP-seq, gene expression, and biochemical data.

claim: IG-DMRmatΔ embryos died soon after E16.
source: Consistent with previous studies, IG-DMRmatΔ embryos died soon after E16 (Lin et al., 2007), so we analyzed MN phenotypes from E10.5~E14.5 in this study.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The expression of Meg3 is still lacking in the developing spinal cord of E14.5 IG-DMRmatΔ embryos.
source: We first verified that the expression of Meg3 is still lacking in the developing spinal cord of E14.5 IG-DMRmatΔ embryos (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Ventral neuronal progenitor patterning was not affected in the IG-DMRmatΔ embryos.
source: Ventral neuronal progenitor patterning was not affected in the IG-DMRmatΔ embryos revealed by Olig2 and Nkx2.2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: A significant increase in the percentage of Pax6on cells (45% penetrance, n = 5/11) was observed for postmitotic MNs (Isl1/2on) along the entire RC axis of the ventral spinal cord in the IG-DMRmatΔ embryos.
source: Compared to the control littermates, we observed a significant increase in the percentage of Pax6on (45% penetrance, n = 5/11), and Irx3on cells (100% penetrance, n = 8/8) for postmitotic MNs (Is11/2on) along the entire RC axis of the ventral spinal cord in the IG-DMRmatΔ embryos (Figure 5A and C, only the cervical segment is shown; quantifications shown in Figure 5B and D).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 5A-D.

claim: A significant increase in the percentage of Irx3on cells (100% penetrance, n = 8/8) was observed for postmitotic MNs (Isl1/2on) along the entire RC axis of the ventral spinal cord in the IG-DMRmatΔ embryos.
source: Compared to the control littermates, we observed a significant increase in the percentage of Pax6on (45% penetrance, n = 5/11), and Irx3on cells (100% penetrance, n = 8/8) for postmitotic MNs (Is11/2on) along the entire RC axis of the ventral spinal cord in the IG-DMRmatΔ embryos (Figure 5A and C, only the cervical segment is shown; quantifications shown in Figure 5B and D).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 5A-D.

claim: Hb9on and Isl1(2)on MNs were comparable between the control and IG-DMRmatΔ embryos at E10.5.
source: However, Hb9on and Isl1(2)on MNs were comparable between the control and IG-DMRmatΔ embryos at E10.5 (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: Production of MNs remained relatively unaffected in IG-DMRmatΔ embryos, suggesting that the generation of MNs is still intact with the co-expressed progenitor/postmitotic genes.
source: Although dorsal progenitor genes were aberrantly up-regulated in the postmitotic MNs, production of MNs remained relatively unaffected, suggesting that the generation of MNs is still intact with the co-expressed progenitor/postmitotic genes in the IG-DMRmatΔ embryos (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that MN numbers are comparable despite ectopic progenitor gene expression.

claim: Comparable numbers of cells expressing respective Hox proteins at each segmental level were observed between control and IG-DMRmatΔ embryos.
source: We observed comparable numbers of cells expressing respective Hox proteins at each segmental level between control and mutant embryos (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: Columnar identities of axial (Lhx3on) and limb-innervating MNs (Foxp1on) were largely unaffected in the IG-DMRmatΔ embryos.
source: Columnar identities of axial (Lhx3on) and limb-innervating MNs (Foxp1on) were also largely unaffected in the IG-DMRmatΔ embryos (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F,G).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F and G.

claim: Hoxc8 was expanded rostrally into Hoxa5on territory in IG-DMRmatΔ embryos.
source: Whereas reciprocal expression of Hoxa5 and Hoxc8 was maintained along the RC axis in the Hox6on LMC MNs of control embryos, Hoxc8 was expanded rostrally into Hoxa5on territory in IG-DMRmatΔ embryos, along with a significant increase of the Hoxc8-mediated downstream motor pool genes, Pea3 and Scip (n = 5 embryos in Figure 6A and C for rostral brachial segments and Figure 6B and D for caudal brachial segments; quantification in Figure 6E and F).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 6A-F.

claim: A significant increase of the Hoxc8-mediated downstream motor pool genes, Pea3 and Scip, was observed in IG-DMRmatΔ embryos.
source: Whereas reciprocal expression of Hoxa5 and Hoxc8 was maintained along the RC axis in the Hox6on LMC MNs of control embryos, Hoxc8 was expanded rostrally into Hoxa5on territory in IG-DMRmatΔ embryos, along with a significant increase of the Hoxc8-mediated downstream motor pool genes, Pea3 and Scip (n = 5 embryos in Figure 6A and C for rostral brachial segments and Figure 6B and D for caudal brachial segments; quantification in Figure 6E and F).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 6A-F.

claim: The reduction of Hoxa5 was not attributable to apoptosis, as cCasp3on cells were comparable in both control and IG-DMRmatΔ mutant embryos.
source: The reduction of Hoxa5 was not attributable to apoptosis, as cCasp3on cells were comparable in both control and IG-DMRmatΔ mutant embryos (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on apoptosis marker staining (data not shown in figures).

claim: The switching of Hoxa5on to Hoxc8on in MNs of IG-DMRmatΔ embryos is not transient, which leads to a concomitant change in motor pool fate.
source: Taken together, the switching of Hoxa5on to Hoxc8on in MNs of IG-DMRmatΔ embryos is not transient, which leads to a concomitant change in motor pool fate (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is inferred from the persistent changes in Hox expression and motor pool markers across developmental stages.

claim: The terminal arbors of suprascapular (Ss) nerves of scapulohumeralis posterior muscles and axillary (Ax) nerves were significantly eroded and reduced in IG-DMRmatΔ embryos.
source: Under higher magnification with better resolution, we observed the terminal arbors of suprascapular (Ss) nerves of scapulohumeralis posterior muscles and axillary (Ax) nerves were significantly eroded and reduced (Figure 7B and C), consistent with the caudalized switch from Hoxa5 to Hoxc8 expression within LMC neurons.
evidence: This is based on light sheet microscopy and Imaris analysis shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: Increased arborization complexity of distal muscle-innervating nerves, including posterior brachial cutaneous (PBC) nerves were manifested in the IG-DMRmatΔ embryos.
source: Concomitantly, increased arborization complexity of distal muscle-innervating nerves, including posterior brachial cutaneous (PBC) nerves were manifested in the IG-DMRmatΔ embryos (Figure 7D, quantification in 7E, n = 6, p<0.01, Mann–Whitney U test).
evidence: This is based on light sheet microscopy and Imaris analysis shown in Figure 7D and E.

claim: The IG-DMRmatΔ mutants displayed deficiencies in peripheral innervation of MNs, which might be a consequence of dysregulation of Hox proteins and/or other axon arborization genes in the absence of lncRNAs from the Dlk1-Dio3 locus.
source: Thus, the IG-DMRmatΔ mutants displayed deficiencies in peripheral innervation of MNs, which might be a consequence of dysregulation of Hox proteins and/or other axon arborization genes in the absence of lncRNAs from the Dlk1-Dio3 locus.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed changes in axon arborization patterns.

claim: In the RianΔ/Δ ESC, expressions of Meg3 and Mirg were relatively unaffected, whereas that of Rian was compromised.
source: We first verified that the paternal gene (i.e., Dlk1) is not affected in either RianΔ/Δ or MirgΔ/Δ ESCs. In the RianΔ/Δ ESC, expressions of Meg3 and Mirg were relatively unaffected, whereas that of Rian was compromised.
evidence: This is based on qPCR data from the CRISPR-generated deletion lines.

claim: Only expression of Mirg was impaired significantly in the MirgΔ/Δ ESCs, but expressions of Meg3 and Rian manifested minimal changes.
source: Conversely, only expression of Mirg was impaired significantly in the MirgΔ/Δ ESCs, but expressions of Meg3 and Rian manifested minimal changes in that cell line (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is based on qPCR data from the CRISPR-generated deletion lines shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Expression of Hoxa5 remained unchanged in the RianΔ/Δ and MirgΔ/Δ ESC~MNs, and Pax6 and Hoxc8 expressions were also unaltered, with similar expression levels to controls.
source: In contrast, expression of Hoxa5 remained unchanged in the RianΔ/Δ and MirgΔ/Δ ESC~MNs, and Pax6 and Hoxc8 expressions were also unaltered, with similar expression levels to controls (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is based on qPCR data from the CRISPR-generated deletion lines shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Meg3 might be the major regulatory lncRNA responsible for the observed MN phenotype displayed by the IG-DMRmatΔ embryos.
source: These results indicate that Meg3 might be the major regulatory lncRNA responsible for the observed MN phenotype displayed by the IG-DMRmatΔ embryos (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of phenotypes between Meg3 KD and Rian/Mirg deletions.

claim: 40% of lncRNAs are expressed specifically in the central nervous system (CNS).
source: Strikingly, 40% of lncRNAs are expressed specifically in the central nervous system (CNS), which makes it one of the best systems for uncovering the physiological functions of lncRNAs (Briggs et al., 2015; Ng et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The paternally-expressed coding gene Dlk1 has an unexpected function in determining MN subtype diversification.
source: and (3) a previous report indicates that the paternally-expressed coding gene Dlk1 has an unexpected function in determining MN subtype diversification (Müller et al., 2014), which prompted us to examine whether the MN-enriched lncRNAs in the same locus also participate in MN cell fate determination.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Meg3 is highly expressed in ESCs.
source: Given that Meg3 is also highly expressed in ESCs (Kaneko et al., 2014a; Mo et al., 2015), we plan to generate a targeted Meg3 floxed allele mouse line in the future that will allow us to specifically knockout Meg3 in MNs and recover the potential function of Meg3 in cell-type specific contexts.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Epigenetic H3K27me3 chromatin modification functions as a legitimate carrier of epigenetic memory.
source: A recent study of Drosophila Hox genes revealed that epigenetic H3K27me3 chromatin modification functions as a legitimate carrier of epigenetic memory (Coleman and Struhl, 2017), providing compelling evidence for a physiologically significant role of chromatin modification in epigenetic inheritance.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: The epigenetic memory carried by H3K27me3 in a postmitotic cell may still be overridden by H3K27me3-opposing demethylases.
source: Nonetheless, the epigenetic memory carried by H3K27me3 in a postmitotic cell may still be overridden by H3K27me3-opposing demethylases (Coleman and Struhl, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Two prominent H3K27me3 demethylases, Kdm6a (Utx) and Kdm6b (Jmjd3), are reactivated in postmitotic MNs.
source: Our RNA-seq data revealed that two prominent H3K27me3 demethylases, Kdm6a (Utx) and Kdm6b (Jmjd3), are reactivated in postmitotic MNs (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data from the study (data not shown in figures).

claim: Removal of Ezh2 from MN progenitors has no detectable impact on segmental Hox expression in the spinal cord (Hoxc6 and Hoxc9).
source: This result also suggests that a compensatory PRC1-mediated function in vivo might make up for the loss of Meg3-mediated epigenetic maintenance in segmental MNs (Golden and Dasen, 2012; Mazzoni et al., 2013b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Many potent miRNA/lncRNA KO mice reflect either only partial phenotype penetrance or more severe phenotypes upon genetic or environmental stresses.
source: Our results are not entirely unexpected as many potent miRNA/lncRNA KO mice reflect either only partial phenotype penetrance (Li et al., 2013; Li et al., 2016; Medeiros et al., 2011), or more severe phenotypes upon genetic or environmental stresses (Williams et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Hypomorphic Suz12-/- ESCs maintained with a low amount of H3K27me3 can differentiate into MNs, albeit with a significant increase in the expression of caudal Hoxc6 and Hoxa7 compared to wild-type cells.
source: A previous study reported that hypomorphic Suz12-/- ESCs maintained with a low amount of H3K27me3 can differentiate into MNs, albeit with a significant increase in the expression of caudal Hoxc6 and Hoxa7 compared to wild-type cells (Mazzoni et al., 2013b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Several PRC2 mutant ESC lines that maintain varying levels of H3K27me3 allowed for proper temporal activation of lineage genes during directed differentiation of ESCs to MNs, but only a subset of the genes that function to specify other lineages were not repressed in these cells.
source: Interestingly, another study found that several PRC2 mutant ESC lines that maintain varying levels of H3K27me3 allowed for proper temporal activation of lineage genes during directed differentiation of ESCs to MNs, but only a subset of the genes that function to specify other lineages were not repressed in these cells (Thornton et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Up-regulated genes in spinal MNs upon loss of Meg3-Rian-Mirg exhibited 50% concordance (3953/7474) with the up-regulated genes in Suz12-/- spinal MNs.
source: In this study, up-regulated genes in spinal MNs upon loss of Meg3-Rian-Mirg exhibited 50% concordance (3953/7474) with the up-regulated genes in Suz12-/- spinal MNs (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on comparison of gene expression data (data not shown in figures).

claim: Hotair -/- mice show partial penetrance of homeotic transformation and increased expression of Meg3.
source: Interestingly, Hotair -/- mice also show partial penetrance of homeotic transformation and increased expression of Meg3 (Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: MEG3 binds to chromatin sites with GA/GT-rich sequences through RNA–DNA triplex formation.
source: Interestingly, a recent report further uncovered that MEG3 binds to chromatin sites with GA/GT-rich sequences through RNA–DNA triplex formation (Iyer et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Two Meg3 knockout mouse lines have previously been generated either by deletion of the first five exons plus approximately 300 bp of the adjacent upstream promoter region of Meg3 (~5.9 kb) or by deletion of ~10 kb that includes the Meg3-DMR region plus the first five exons of Meg3.
source: Specifically, two Meg3 knockout mouse lines have previously been generated either by deletion of the first five exons plus approximately 300 bp of the adjacent upstream promoter region of Meg3 (~5.9 kb) (Zhou et al., 2010) or by deletion of ~10 kb that includes the Meg3-DMR region plus the first five exons of Meg3 (Takahashi et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Both Meg3 KO lines manifested loss of maternal Rian and Mirg lncRNA expression.
source: Both of these Meg3 KO lines also manifested loss of maternal Rian and Mirg lncRNA expression.
evidence: This is based on findings from previous studies.

claim: The ~5.9 kb Meg3 KO line exhibited perinatal lethality.
source: However, whereas the ~5.9 kb Meg3 KO line (Zhou et al., 2010) exhibited perinatal lethality, the ~10 kb Meg3 KO line (Takahashi et al., 2009) presented a much milder phenotype in that the mice were born alive and lived up to 4 weeks after birth.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: The ~10 kb Meg3 KO line presented a much milder phenotype in that the mice were born alive and lived up to 4 weeks after birth.
source: However, whereas the ~5.9 kb Meg3 KO line (Zhou et al., 2010) exhibited perinatal lethality, the ~10 kb Meg3 KO line (Takahashi et al., 2009) presented a much milder phenotype in that the mice were born alive and lived up to 4 weeks after birth.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Deletions of Rian and Mirg show less profound phenotype than upstream Meg3.
source: Consistent with previous results (Han et al., 2014; Labialle et al., 2014), deletions of these downstream lncRNAs show less profound phenotype than upstream Meg3.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies and is consistent with the current study's findings.

claim: Mirg KO embryos seem to have a less severe phenotype, and no observed homeotic transformation has been reported.
source: Interestingly, Mirg KO embryos seem to have a less severe phenotype, and no observed homeotic transformation has been reported (Labialle et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Mirg does not bind to Ezh2/Suz12/Jarid2.
source: Furthermore, our results indicate that Mirg does not bind to Ezh2/Suz12/Jarid2 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on RIP data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Epimutations (hypermethylations) and microdeletions affecting IG-DMR and/or MEG3-DMR of maternal origin result in a unique human phenotype manifested as a small bell-shaped thorax, coat-hanger-like appearance of the ribs, abdominal wall defects, placentomegaly and polyhydramnios, termed 'Kagami-Ogata syndrome' (KOS).
source: Consistent with the imprinting status of the DLK1-DIO3 locus in humans, epimutations (hypermethylations) and microdeletions affecting IG-DMR and/or MEG3-DMR of maternal origin result in a unique human phenotype manifested as a small bell-shaped thorax, coat-hanger-like appearance of the ribs, abdominal wall defects, placentomegaly and polyhydramnios. One hallmark of patients with this disease, termed 'Kagami-Ogata syndrome' (KOS) (Kagami et al., 2015; Ogata and Kagami, 2016), is that nearly all of them display delayed gross motor development.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies on KOS.

claim: Nearly all KOS patients display delayed gross motor development.
source: One hallmark of patients with this disease, termed 'Kagami-Ogata syndrome' (KOS) (Kagami et al., 2015; Ogata and Kagami, 2016), is that nearly all of them display delayed gross motor development.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies on KOS.

claim: Extra ossification at the sites where the 6th to 8th ribs attach to the sternum was observed in IG-DMRmatΔ embryos, similar to the malformed thorax in KOS patients.
source: In our IG-DMRmatΔ embryos, we previously observed extra ossification at the sites where the 6th to 8th ribs attach to the sternum, similar to the malformed thorax in KOS patients (Lin et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Extra ossification at the sites where the 6th to 8th ribs attach to the sternum was also observed in Hox5 mutant mouse embryos.
source: Interestingly, this phenotype was also observed in Hox5 mutant mouse embryos (McIntyre et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Loss of Meg3 in vitro and in vivo abrogates the Hoxa5on MNs in the brachial region, with a concomitant increase of ectopic Hoxc8on subtypes.
source: Here, we uncovered that two isoforms of the Meg3 imprinted lncRNA are enriched in embryonic MNs and confer the fidelity of the epigenetic landscape for the Hoxa5-Hoxc8 boundary of MN subtypes. Loss of Meg3 in vitro and in vivo abrogates the Hoxa5on MNs in the brachial region, with a concomitant increase of ectopic Hoxc8on subtypes.
evidence: This is a summary of key findings from the study.

claim: The switch from Hoxa5 to Hoxc8 leads to erosion of Hoxa5on motor axon arborization in the proximal muscles.
source: This switch leads to erosion of Hoxa5on motor axon arborization in the proximal muscles.
evidence: This is based on light sheet microscopy data showing changes in axon arborization.

claim: Impairment of the Hox boundary mediated by Meg3 in the spinal cord and ribs might account for the bell-shaped thorax and motor deficit in KOS patients.
source: As Meg3 expression is also highly enriched in somites, we suggest that impairment of the Hox boundary mediated by Meg3 in the spinal cord and ribs might account for the bell-shaped thorax and motor deficit in KOS patients, potentially identifying a new therapeutic target for KOS patients.
evidence: This is a speculative inference connecting the mouse findings to human disease.

claim: Meg3 is important for proper growth and development and is a putative tumor suppressor that activates p53 and inhibits cell proliferation.
source: In addition to the roles of the Meg3 imprinted lncRNA uncovered by our study, other reports have also emphasized Meg3 as being important for proper growth and development and to be a putative tumor suppressor that activates p53 and inhibits cell proliferation (Takahashi et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Aberrant repression of Meg3 and other maternally-expressed lncRNAs from the DLK1-DIO3 imprinting cluster is present in several induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) lines.
source: Moreover, aberrant repression of Meg3 and other maternally-expressed lncRNAs from the DLK1-DIO3 imprinting cluster is present in several induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) lines.
evidence: This is established knowledge about iPSCs.

claim: Aberrant repression of Meg3 and other maternally-expressed lncRNAs from the DLK1-DIO3 imprinting cluster might lead to failure of iPSCs to form viable mice or to efficiently differentiate into neural lineage cells.
source: This scenario might lead to failure of these iPSCs to form viable mice (Stadtfeld et al., 2010) or to efficiently differentiate into neural lineage cells (Mo et al., 2015), raising the possibility that Meg3 might be involved in a broad spectrum of developmental processes and disease contexts.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.
